::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Extra dependencies required

Network support depends on `mikeio1d`, which reads the result files and builds
the network, and which is **not** installed by default. Install it alongside
`modelskill` with the _network_ extra:

```bash
uv pip install modelskill[network]
```

or 

```bash
uv add modelskill[network]
```

:::

```{python}
# | echo: false

path_to_res1d = "../../tests/testdata/network.res1d"
path_to_sensor_data_1 = "../../tests/testdata/network_sensor_1.csv"
path_to_sensor_data_2 = "../../tests/testdata/network_sensor_2.csv"
path_to_sensor_data_4 = "../../tests/testdata/network_sensor_4.csv"
```

A **network** is a 1D pipe or river network read as a graph: nodes hold timeseries
data (water level at a junction, say), reaches carry the topology and the length
between them, and break points along a reach are locations in their own right.

The workflow is the usual four steps, with the network standing in for a grid or a
mesh:

```
result file  →  NetworkModelResult  →  match()  →  Comparer
```

## Where the network comes from

Reading the file and building the graph is [mikeio1d](https://github.com/DHI/mikeio1d)'s
job, not modelskill's. `Network.open` reads MIKE 1D (`.res1d`), MIKE 11 (`.res11`)
and EPANET (`.res`) results, finds the EPANET companion files, and says so when a
format cannot be turned into a network. See its documentation for the companions,
and for `resolve`, which looks up a location by the name the model gives it.

modelskill takes the file path directly, and opens it for you:

```{python}
import modelskill as ms

mr = ms.NetworkModelResult(path_to_res1d, name="MyModel", item="WaterLevel")
mr
```

A model result reads no timeseries when it is built. Each observation's location is
read when it is matched, and only that location, so scoring a few sensors against a
large model reads a few series.

Open the network yourself when you need to name EPANET companion files, or to build
model results for several quantities over one network:

```{python}
from mikeio1d.network import Network

network = Network.open(path_to_res1d)
ms.NetworkModelResult(network, name="MyModel", item="WaterLevel")
```

## Skill assessment workflow

### 1. The model result

`mr` above is the model side of the comparison, for one quantity. It reads a
location when an observation is matched there.

### 2. Create NodeObservations and compute skill

`NodeObservation` accepts a file path directly; the observation name is taken from the filename.

The `at=` argument takes either of two forms, depending on what you have at hand.

::: {.callout-note}
## MIKE 1D vocabulary vs the modelskill API
In MIKE 1D, "nodes" are the named connection points in the 1D network (manholes, junctions, outfalls) while "reaches" are the pipe or channel segments that connect them.  The modelskill API uses `NodeObservation` more broadly: the `at=` argument accepts either the node's name **or** a `(reach_id, position)` break point tuple that identifies a specific chainage along a reach.  If you only need a reach-level quantity (uniform across the reach), use `ReachObservation` with `reach=` instead.
:::

#### Option A — the node's name

Pass the node's name in the model, e.g. the Res1D node name. It is resolved against the network at match time:

```{python}
obs_1 = ms.NodeObservation(path_to_sensor_data_1, at="98")

cc = ms.match(obs=obs_1, mod=mr)
cc.skill()
```

::: {.callout-note}
Resolution happens inside `ms.match()`.  A name the network does not hold raises a `ValueError`.
:::

#### Option B — breakpoint by `(reach, position)` tuple

When your observation sits at a chainage along a reach rather than at a named junction node, you can use the `at` argument and pass a `(reach_id, position)` tuple.  The `NetworkModelResult` looks up the corresponding breakpoint at match time:

```{python}
obs_bp = ms.NodeObservation(path_to_sensor_data_2, at=("117l1", 48.7))

cc = ms.match(obs=obs_bp, mod=mr)
cc.skill()
```

The tuple form is resolved during matching, as `network.resolve(("117l1", 48.7))` would resolve it.

::: {.callout-note}
## Chainage tolerance

By default a position matches a break point within the tolerance mikeio1d uses to decide two chainages are the same place, which absorbs floating-point rounding between the position you type and the value stored in the network.  A measured chainage is rarely that close; pass `position_tol=` to snap it onto the nearest break point within that distance that carries the item being scored:

```python
obs_bp = ms.NodeObservation(path_to_sensor_data_2, at=("117l1", 48.0), position_tol=1.0)
```

The comparer keeps the chainage you gave; `cc.raw_mod_data["MyModel"].at` gives the break point the model was read at.  If no break point falls within the tolerance, a `ValueError` says the location is not found and points to `network.addresses(reach=...)`, which lists the break points along that reach.  One is raised too when the location exists but carries no data for the quantity you are scoring - MIKE 1D stores water level and discharge at alternating grid points along a reach.
:::

### 3. Using ReachObservation for reach-uniform quantities

Some physical quantities — such as **discharge in a pipe** — are conceptually uniform across the whole reach, even though the model stores values at individual breakpoints along the reach. `ReachObservation` lets you associate a timeseries with a named reach without having to identify a specific breakpoint.

When matched against a `NetworkModelResult`, modelskill extracts model data from the breakpoints on the given reach that carry the quantity and hold data for it. When there are several, they must carry equivalent values, and the one with the lowest position is used.

```{python}
obs_q = ms.ReachObservation(path_to_sensor_data_4, reach="116l1", name="Q_116l1")
obs_q
```

Pass the observation to `ms.match()` exactly as you would a `NodeObservation`. modelskill resolves which breakpoint to use automatically:

```{python}
mr_q = ms.NetworkModelResult(network, name="MyModel", item="Discharge")
cc_q = ms.match(obs=obs_q, mod=mr_q)
cc_q.skill()
```

::: {.callout-note}
Use `ReachObservation` when your measured quantity is representative of the whole reach (e.g. discharge, which is constant along a reach in steady flow).  If you need to compare a quantity that varies spatially along the reach (e.g. water level at a specific chainage), use a `NodeObservation` with a `(reach, position)` tuple instead (see [Option B](#option-b-breakpoint-by-reach-position-tuple) above).
:::
